Neonatal giant otters emerge weighing approximately 350 grams [Wwb = approximately 350 grams], a modest body mass that belies their rapid growth trajectory under the intense biparental care characteristic of the species. Pups are born in dens dug into riverbanks, typically during the dry season when water levels are receding and prey availability is high. The gestation period lasts 68 days [tg = 68 days] when the mother maintains a stable core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a relatively brief developmental interval for a mustelid of this body size. Litter sizes range from one to five cubs, with two being the modal number across most studied populations in the Amazon and Pantanal regions. The high maternal investment is evident from the first days of life, as the altricial neonates are entirely dependent on milk and maternal warmth. Weaning occurs at 122 days after birth [tx = 122 days after birth] under the same thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], at which point the pups begin accompanying the adults on foraging excursions and consuming solid prey items.

Females attain sexual maturity at approximately 730 days after birth [tp = approximately 730 days after birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a developmental milestone that coincides with the achievement of nearly full adult skeletal dimensions. This relatively delayed puberty, characteristic of many long-lived social carnivores, is thought to reflect the extended period required for learning complex cooperative hunting techniques and establishing a stable social position within the natal group. Males typically mature slightly later, although precise field data remain sparse due to the difficulty of tracking dispersing individuals. The age at first reproduction for females generally follows closely after the onset of puberty, with most documented first litters occurring between two and three years of age. Reproductive output is constrained by the availability of stable den sites and the density of fish prey in the territory. The maximum reproductive rate observed in wild populations has been decomposed into a modal litter size of approximately 1.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 1.5 pups per litter], with females producing a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], a modest fecundity reflecting the intensive investment per offspring and the extended duration of parental care typical of this apex predator.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in the giant otter, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 24,000 grams [Wwi = 24,000 grams], while males are substantially larger, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 29,000 grams [Wwi = 29,000 grams]. These values place Pteronura brasiliensis among the largest of the mustelids, exceeded in mass only by the marine otter and the sea otter. The dimorphism is thought to be related to male-male competition for territories and access to breeding females, as larger males are better able to defend prime stretches of riverine habitat that support abundant fish stocks. Field studies in the Pantanal have recorded adult males occasionally exceeding 30,000 grams, though 29,000 grams [Wwi = 29,000 grams] is considered representative for the species across its range. Females typically range between 22,000 and 26,000 grams, with 24,000 grams [Wwi = 24,000 grams] serving as a reliable benchmark for comparative life-history analyses. The attainment of adult mass requires sustained high feeding rates throughout the juvenile and sub-adult periods.

Longevity in the giant otter is substantial for a mustelid, recorded in the wild when the animal maintains a core temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], with a maximum lifespan of approximately 17.3 years [am = approximately 17.3 years]. This extended lifespan is typical of large-bodied carnivores with complex social structures and low natural mortality rates once adulthood is reached. Wild individuals face threats from jaguar predation, habitat destruction, and conflict with fishermen, yet in protected areas, annual adult survival rates exceed 80 percent. Captive specimens in well-managed zoological institutions have occasionally surpassed 19 years, underscoring the species' inherent physiological capacity for extended survival. The senescence pattern involves gradual declines in hunting efficiency and tooth wear rather than acute reproductive cessation, with some females successfully rearing litters into their fourteenth year. Comparative analyses within the Lutrinae suggest that the giant otter's longevity exceeds that of the Eurasian otter by several years.

The reproductive strategy of the giant otter is characterized by the production of a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], with the female entering oestrus shortly after the previous litter is weaned. Combining the modal litter size of 1.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1.5 pups per litter] with the annual frequency of one litter [F_R_i = annual frequency of one litter] yields an annual reproductive output that is low but consistent with the species' slow life-history pace and extended parental investment. The timing of birth is closely tied to seasonal flooding cycles, with most births occurring between May and October in the Amazon basin when fish are concentrated in shrinking water bodies. This synchrony ensures that the energetically demanding late lactation and weaning phases coincide with peak prey densities. The family group, comprising the mated pair and offspring from one or two seasons, cooperatively defends a territory that may extend for several kilometers along a river course, a social system that further limits the density of breeding females per unit area.
